notes.meaning: Manasseh took the throne in Jerusalem when he was only twelve years old. He went on to rule for fifty-five years, which was the longest reign of any king of Judah. Because his father Hezekiah had received fifteen extra years of life from God, Manasseh was born during that granted time. A young ruler without wise guidance can easily be led down dangerous paths.

Manasseh rejected the true God and chose to live in open wickedness. He copied the shameful religious customs of the pagan nations whom the Lord had driven out of Canaan centuries earlier. God had cleared the land so His people could live holy lives, but Manasseh welcomed those very evils back into Judah.

Manasseh tore down the good work of his father Hezekiah by rebuilding the outdoor pagan worship sites. He built altars to the false god Baal, set up a wooden pole to honor the goddess Asherah, and worshiped the sun, moon, and stars. In doing this, he acted just like King Ahab, one of the most wicked kings in Israel's history.

Manasseh placed pagan altars right inside the temple of the Lord. The Lord had chosen this sacred building in Jerusalem as the special dwelling place for His holy Name. Putting idols into God's own house was a direct, defiant insult to the living God.

The king expanded this false worship across the entire temple complex. He built altars for the stars and heavenly bodies in both the inner courtyard of the priests and the outer courtyard of the people. Sacred spaces meant for prayer and sacrifice were turned into centers of star worship.

Manasseh sank into terrible cruelty by burning his own son as a sacrifice to a false god. He also practiced fortune-telling, cast spells, and consulted people who claimed to speak with the dead. These dark practices completely broke God's law and stirred up the Lord's righteous anger.

Manasseh made a carved image of the pagan goddess Asherah and placed it inside the holy temple. God had promised King David and his son Solomon that this temple would be the permanent earthly home for His Name. Setting up a filthy idol where God alone was to be honored was the lowest point of the king's rebellion.

The Lord reminded the nation of His ancient covenant promise. He had pledged that Israel would never be driven from the Promised Land as long as they obeyed all the laws Moses gave them. Their safety and peace in the land always depended on their faithful obedience to God.

The people of Judah refused to listen to God and followed their king into spiritual ruin. Manasseh led them so far into evil that they became worse than the pagan nations God had destroyed before them. Having God's law made their deliberate choice of sin even more terrible.

The Lord did not leave the people without warning in their dark times. He sent His faithful prophets to speak His truth and call the nation back from destruction. Even when the culture turned against God, His voice still called out to them.

The prophets declared God's formal charge against Manasseh. He had committed worse sins than the ancient Amorites who lived in the land before Israel arrived. By his royal power and bad example, he had dragged the entire nation of Judah into idolatry.

The Lord announced that a terrible disaster was coming upon Jerusalem and Judah. The news of this judgment would be so shocking that anyone hearing it would feel their ears ring in disbelief. God's patience had reached its limit, and holy justice was about to fall.

God warned that He would use the same strict standard of judgment against Jerusalem that He had used to destroy the northern capital of Samaria and Ahab's family. He used the picture of a person wiping a bowl completely clean and turning it upside down. Jerusalem would be thoroughly cleared of its inhabitants and left empty.

The Lord declared that He would abandon the remaining tribes of Judah and Benjamin, which were the remnant of His people. He would surrender them into the hands of foreign invaders to be captured and looted. Sin strips away divine protection and leaves a nation defenseless.

This terrible judgment was not sparked by Manasseh's sins alone, but by a long history of national unfaithfulness. Israel had provoked the Lord repeatedly ever since He brought their ancestors out of slavery in Egypt. Centuries of ignored warnings and repeated idolatry had finally brought them to this breaking point.

Along with his idolatry, Manasseh ruled as a violent tyrant and murdered countless innocent people throughout Jerusalem. Ancient tradition says this slaughter included God's prophets who spoke out against his evil, including the prophet Isaiah. The king stained the holy city with the blood of the righteous from one end to the other.

The rest of Manasseh's official royal records were written down in the historical annals of Judah's kings. While this book focuses on his sins to explain why the exile had to come, the book of Chronicles later records that he was captured by Assyria and truly repented before God. God's mercy can reach even the worst sinner who turns to Him.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: An ancient prayer called the Prayer of Manasseh, based on the king's repentance described in 2 Chronicles, is included in ancient Greek copies of the Old Testament and is read in Eastern Orthodox worship services.

notes.meaning: Manasseh died after his long reign and was buried in his private palace garden, known as the garden of Uzza. Unlike faithful kings before him, he was not laid to rest in the royal tombs of David's line. His son Amon succeeded him on the throne.

Amon was twenty-two years old when he became king, and his reign in Jerusalem lasted only two years. His mother was Meshullemeth from the town of Jotbah. His short time on the throne mirrored the brief reigns of many wicked rulers in Israel's history.

Amon committed evil in the eyes of the Lord, copying the terrible pattern of his father Manasseh. He followed all of his father's wicked practices, but he never shared in his father's later humility or repentance. Choosing to copy a parent's sin without learning from their pain always leads to ruin.

Amon walked in all the corrupt paths his father had laid out before him. He brought back the worship of the very idols that Manasseh had set up earlier in his life. Bad examples often leave deep roots that are hard for the next generation to break.

Amon turned his back completely on the Lord, the God of his ancestors David and Solomon. He refused to obey God's commands or walk in His ways. Walking away from God left him without divine protection or wisdom.

Amon's own palace officials plotted against him and murdered him inside his home. Because he had filled God's house with idols, God allowed his own palace to be stained with his blood. His unfaithfulness brought sudden violence right into his private rooms.

The regular citizens of Judah rose up, executed the conspirators who had murdered the king, and placed Amon's young son Josiah on the throne. By doing this, the people preserved the royal family line of David as God had promised. Out of this dark period of murder and chaos, God was preparing one of Judah's greatest and most faithful kings.

The rest of what Amon did during his short reign was recorded in the official chronicles of Judah's kings. His life was brief and marked only by disobedience, offering a tragic warning about a wasted life.

Amon was buried in his tomb in the garden of Uzza, placed beside his father instead of with the honored kings of Judah. His eight-year-old son Josiah then began his reign. God's faithfulness remained steady, bringing a dawn of spiritual renewal through young Josiah.
